leads.title: Small daily habit changes could add years to your life, study finds
leads.summary: A University of Sydney study published in eClinicalMedicine on January 13, 2026 followed more than 59,000 older adults in the UK Biobank for just over eight years. People with the poorest habits who made three small changes together - about 5 more minutes of sleep a night, about 2 more minutes of exercise a day and a small diet improvement - gained about one year of life. Bigger but still modest changes (24 more minutes of sleep, under 4 more minutes of exercise, better diet) were linked to up to four more years free of serious disease such as heart disease, cancer, dementia or type 2 diabetes. Researchers say to start with small, realistic steps.
leads.source: Powers Health / University of Sydney study

leads.title: A Kargil teacher turns old war bunkers into classrooms where children can live history
leads.summary: Mohd Mustafa Kamal, a 41-year-old teacher from Wakha village near Kargil in Ladakh, converted a derelict military bunker at his school into a history lab called the Cave Classroom, so students can feel history instead of only reading it. He also made a Museum Classroom with local artefacts and a parliament-style seating plan for civics. He received the National Teachers Award 2026 from President Droupadi Murmu on September 5, 2026, among 48 teachers honoured. Innovator Sonam Wangchuk praised his bottom-up approach.

leads.title: Berlin mapped 900,000 street trees. Now 12,000 people water them.
leads.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Amanda Gläser-Bligh named her street tree Linda. Linda is a linden, eight years old, growing outside Gläser-Bligh’s apartment building in Charlottenburg, and once a week during Berlin’s hot months, Gläser-Bligh makes a couple of trips up and down the stairs with a watering can until she has carried 20 liters (about five gallons) of water to Linda’s roots. Passersby sometimes stop and stare. They usually end up asking what she’s doing, and most of them, once they find out, look up at the tree a little differently. Berlin has nearly a million street trees, and like cities across Europe, it’s watching them struggle through increasingly hot summers. A project called Gieß den Kiez , which translates to “water your neighborhood” in German, is trying to close the gap between what the city’s maintenance crews can do and what the trees need, by giving ordinary people a map, a reason, and a social framework for showing up with a watering can. Twelve thousand people have signed up. 900,000 trees color-coded by thirst and updated in real time Developed by CityLAB Berlin , the Gieß den Kiez app tracks more than 900,000 trees across the city and calculates each tree’s water needs based on its age, species, and local rainfall. Color-coding shows which trees are in critical condition. Saplings, which lack the deep root networks of mature trees, need more frequent watering to survive and are flagged accordingly. Volunteers can log a watering, see when a tree was last watered by someone else, and find the locations of Berlin’s public water pumps. leads.title: The Hospital That Silenced the Machines
leads.summary: B eep. Beep. Beep. The heartbeat monitor chirps. Hospitals have long tried to fight acoustic chaos with passive tactics — hanging sound-absorbing ceiling tiles, laying soft rubber flooring or begging clinical staff to whisper in the corridors. Beep. Beep. Beep. Blood pressure drops. But the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust in the United Kingdom has been trying something different. Instead of regarding noise as an inevitable physical nuisance that needs to be muffled, it treats sound as data that can be routed. In 2023, the trust launched the Silent Hospital Pilot Project , a three-year study exploring how to target “alarm fatigue” and noise pollution on hospital wards. As the second phase of the pilot comes to an end, its outcomes have already been so promising that other hospital networks around the U.K. are preparing to follow suit. Beep. Beep. Beep. Oxygen levels dip. Hospital wards are notoriously loud, with continuous background noise on intensive care units , for example, often averaging 50 to 70 decibels (dB), comparable to heavy traffic, and sharp peaks frequently passing 80 to 100 dB, roughly the equivalent of a jackhammer. These levels vastly exceed the World Health Organization’s recommended threshold of 30 dB to be able to rest. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. The monitor escalates to an urgent, repeating multi-tone musical sequence engineered to demand immediate human attention. Studies across international health systems reveal that clinical staff encounter hundreds of alarm signals per shift, up to 90 percent of which require no clinical intervention, for example because a patient mistakenly presses the buzzer when they move. leads.title: A Place to Sleep for Denver’s Homeless College Students
leads.summary: This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters. During her first semester at Chicago’s Malcolm X College, Nikya Harrell had had enough. It was winter, and she was cold. She was bouncing to and from family members’ houses and sometimes could only afford one meal a week. Harrell came to school overwhelmed and crying. A concerned friend suggested she see the school’s therapist, who connected her with the Dax Program, which offers students at risk of or experiencing homelessness a place to live for up to two years. Harrell came to Denver for Depaul USA’s Dax Program’s recent opening of the city’s first student residence near the Capitol building. Harrell had a message for other students who face challenges finding a place to live that she’s often repeated to herself: “You’re never alone.” Community members gather to bless the newly opened Depaul USA Dax Program housing on September 24, 2026, in Denver. Credit: Jason Gonzales / Chalkbeat Dax provides students with a safe living space that allows them to focus on getting a college degree without worrying about where they’ll sleep. The program has partnered with Metropolitan State University of Denver and Regis University, but wants to expand services to other local colleges and universities. The nonprofit provides resources to people experiencing homelessness and operates 11 Dax student housing programs in Chicago, Los Angeles, Philadelphia and New York. The program started in 2015 and has housed 494 students in those cities. The Denver Dax residence, an 1890s brick building that was originally a duplex in North Capitol Hill, is one of the national program’s larger residences and will be able to house up to 15 students.
